KL divergence

Lesson 80 needed a way to say how far apart two policies are. The Kullback–Leibler divergence is that measure: the average extra surprise from using $q$ when outcomes really follow $p$. It is never negative, it is zero only when $p = q$, and swapping $p$ and $q$ changes it.

KL from samples

KL is an average under $p$, so it can be estimated without summing over every outcome: sample $x \sim p$ and average $\log p(x) / q(x)$. Language models (Lesson 88) have far too many outcomes to sum, so this is how they do it.

The maths

For distributions $p$ and $q$ over the same outcomes,

$$\begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) &= \sum_x p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\!\left[\log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right] \end{aligned}$$

It is the average, over outcomes drawn from $p$, of how much more likely $p$ found them than $q$ did. With the natural log the unit is nats. Terms with $p(x) = 0$ count as 0.

Never negative (Gibbs' inequality). $\log$ is concave, so Jensen's inequality $\mathbb{E}[\log Z] \le \log \mathbb{E}[Z]$ gives

$$\begin{aligned} -D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) &= \mathbb{E}_{p}\!\left[\log \frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\right] \le \log \mathbb{E}_{p}\!\left[\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\right] \\ &= \log \sum_{x:\,p(x)>0} q(x) \le \log 1 = 0 \end{aligned}$$

Equality needs $q(x)/p(x)$ to be constant, so $D_{\mathrm{KL}} = 0$ exactly when $p = q$.

Not symmetric. In general $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) \ne D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \,\|\, p)$, so it is not a distance in the strict sense. If $q(x) = 0$ where $p(x) > 0$, the term $p(x) \log(p(x)/0)$ is infinite: $q$ calls impossible something that happens.

Small changes. Let $q = p + \Delta$ with $\sum_x \Delta(x) = 0$. Using $\log(1+u) \approx u - u^2/2$,

$$\begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, p + \Delta) &= -\sum_x p(x)\log\!\Big(1 + \frac{\Delta(x)}{p(x)}\Big) \\ &\approx -\sum_x \Delta(x) + \frac12\sum_x \frac{\Delta(x)^2}{p(x)} = \frac12 \sum_x \frac{\Delta(x)^2}{p(x)} \end{aligned}$$

Nearby, KL is a squared distance where each change is divided by the probability it changes. Moving an outcome from $0.01$ to $0.02$ costs far more than moving one from $0.50$ to $0.51$. That is the policy-space distance Lesson 80 asked for. For policies it is applied state by state: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot \mid s) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{new}}(\cdot \mid s)\big)$, and TRPO bounds its average over visited states.
